title: Temperature-dependent larval survival and development in Petrolisthes japonicus (De Haan, 1849) (Decapoda: Anomura: Porcellanidae)
content:
Abstract
Temperature is a major environmental factor affecting larval survival and development in marine decapod crustaceans. We investigated the effects of temperature on larval survival and development in the porcellanid crab Petrolisthes japonicus (De Haan, 1849). Larvae from two broods were individually reared at five temperatures (20°C, 23°C, 26°C, 29°C, and 32°C) from hatching to the first crab stage. Survival from each larval stage to the subsequent stage was evaluated using logistic equations, and developmental rates were evaluated using heat-summation equations. Survival responses differed among larval stages. First zoeae successfully molted to second zoeae at all temperatures, whereas survival of second zoeae declined markedly at 32°C and megalopal survival decreased substantially at 20°C. Intermolt periods and the total developmental period decreased significantly with increasing temperature and were well described by heat-summation equations. Lower threshold temperature for development tended to be higher for megalopae than for zoeal stages. These results indicate stage-specific temperature-dependent patterns in larval survival and development. Such differences may reflect the thermal conditions encountered by different larval stages during the reproductive season. Estimated developmental periods based on regional sea surface temperature suggest that the period favorable for larval development may be longer along the Pacific coast than near the northern distribution limit of the species on the Sea of Japan coast. These findings provide insight into ecological factors influencing larval survival and development and contribute to understanding the temporal and spatial conditions that shape the geographic distribution of P. japonicus.
